title: Legal Tech for Non-Lawyers: Report of the Survey of US Legal Technologies
pub: American Bar Foundation research report (with the assistance of Alice Chang, Taemesha Hyder, Sajid Khurram, Elizabeth Prete, Matthew Schneider, and Noah Tate); funded by the Open Society Foundations
author: Rebecca L. Sandefur

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The supplied excerpt contains only funding and acknowledgement information. It provides no substantive findings or arguments about whether cheaper legal assistance increases participation without improving remedies, so the source’s position relative to the cluster cannot be determined.

st.t: Justice gap: Fair resolution exceeds legal assistance
st.an: The source accepts the broad population-level framing of justice need and materially extends it by identifying immigration and criminal-justice problems omitted from typical civil surveys. It also reinforces that existing legal technologies provide only narrow forms of assistance, so tool availability should not be equated with fair resolution.
qs: Tools do exist that offer some assistance in the areas of law where Americans most commonly experience justice problems, but the services they offer for those problems are limited, focused mainly on providing legal information, referring users to attorneys, and creating different kinds of documents.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s practical focus and materially strengthens its access-to-justice analysis with survey evidence that many non-lawyer tools exclude users through English-only and text-dependent design. Its catalogue of tool capabilities without demonstrated legal outcomes also reinforces the distinction between product claims and reliable service delivery.
qs: Fully 75% of existing tools require English-language facility.
Only 16% of tools provide at least some of the material offered though a means other than written text, such as a video.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s selective-deployment and access-to-justice claims: its 2018 survey finds that legal technologies generally automate fragmented tasks rather than provide end-to-end resolution, and that meaningful value depends on matching tools to user needs and overcoming regulatory and institutional barriers. Its evidence predates generative AI, so it does not directly establish current model capability, verification needs or lawyer–AI divisions of labour.
qs: For example, there is no tool that consists of a natural language interface that diagnoses the legal aspects of a user’s life situation, offers possible routes to solution, and then facilitates taking action toward a solution by compiling evidence of a complaint and creating or filing a legal document with a court or other agency.

Source: Survey of US Legal Technologies  WHAT TOOLS PROVIDE VERSUS WHAT PEOPLE WANT OR NEED  There is a substantial mismatch between the services tools offer and what is known about the assistance wanted or needed by the American public.

kp.k: Survey establishes a Fall 2018 nonlawyer technology baseline
kp.d: The survey identified 322 technologies for nonlawyer users in US jurisdictions, including members of the public and professionals assisting them. Researchers screened just over 600 unique technologies identified through existing lists, app-store searches and practitioner outreach, coding service areas, functions and accessibility. This is a descriptive survey of digital legal technologies generally, not a study specifically of AI or its effects; the report explicitly disclaims comprehensive coverage.
qs: The Survey reports on the state of the field as of Fall 2018.
The Survey identified 322 technologies designed for use by non-lawyers in US jurisdictions
While this project’s strategy for identifying the universe of such technologies was expansive, no such effort can claim to be comprehensive.

kp.k: Information and referrals dominate nonlawyer legal tools
kp.d: About three quarters of tools provided legal information and just under half connected users to attorneys. Most referrals were cold lists selected by location or specialty; about 15% of tools offered warm referrals that transferred potential-client information. Sandefur finds that most tools supplied limited services rather than supporting independent problem resolution.
qs: About three quarters of tools provide legal information of some type, and just under half connect people to attorneys.
About 15% of tools offer “warm” referrals, where the tool passes along information about the potential client and connects the client with the attorney.
The modal tool does little to facilitate a nonlawyer in taking any independent action on a justice problem.

kp.k: Action-enabling tools primarily automate document production
kp.d: The survey found 167 technologies facilitating action without attorney assistance, or 52% of all tools. Among these, 70% created documents and a fifth helped compile evidence. Diagnosis, online dispute resolution and crowdfunding were rare. Tools typically automated an individual task rather than an integrated problem-solving process.
qs: Just over half of tools (52%) assist the user in taking some action on a justice problem, such as producing a legal document, compiling evidence, diagnosing a legal problem, or resolving a dispute.
As Figure 2 reports, 70% of tools that “do” something, create documents.
A fifth of this group of tools help users compile evidence

kp.d: As of the survey period, the report found no general-purpose tool combining natural-language diagnosis, solution options, evidence compilation and document creation or filing. A few tools supported a fuller sequence within a specific problem area: JustFix, for example, helped assemble and send landlord complaints about habitability.
qs: No existing tool is a “one stop shop” for justice problems generally.
These tools take a user from identifying a problem, to considering options, to taking action on it themselves.
For example, JustFix assists users in putting together a complaint to a landlord about a habitability problem in an apartment, and then sends the complaint letter.

kp.k: Legal coverage only partly matches public justice needs
kp.d: Of 322 tools, 51% served criminal matters, 31% family, 25% consumer, 23% real estate, 23% civil rights, 22% employment, 22% housing and 21% health; 22% claimed to serve any area of law. The report compares coverage with civil-justice surveys identifying household finances, health and insurance, consumer, family, livelihood and housing problems as common. It qualifies this comparison because those surveys typically excluded immigration and criminal involvement, and stresses that available functions remain limited even where subject coverage exists.
qs: About a fifth of tools (22%) claim to assist users with problems in any area of law.
The types of justice problems served by the tools, while often important, only partly match the types of justice problems most commonly reported by Americans.

Tools do exist that offer some assistance in the areas of law where Americans most commonly experience justice problems, but the services they offer for those problems are limited, focused mainly on providing legal information, referring users to attorneys, and creating different kinds of documents.

kp.k: Unrecognized legal problems create an unmet diagnostic need
kp.d: Drawing on prior civil-justice research, Sandefur argues that people frequently do not recognize the legal dimensions or remedies associated with everyday problems. Document creation therefore intervenes too late for many needs, after users have already identified a legal problem and a formal response. She proposes diagnosis and response options as potentially particularly valuable, while finding very few such tools.
qs: Since most Americans facing justice problems do not recognize legal aspects of their problems, existing tools are not useful for most problems.

In a context where many people experience justice problems that they do not recognize as legal or remediable, tools that offer diagnosis – explaining to someone that their problem involves specific legal aspects, such as violations of housing codes or wage and hour laws – and provide options for response could be particularly valuable.
There are very few such tools.

kp.k: Internet inequalities restrict digital access to justice
kp.d: Citing Pew, the report states that 89% of US adults used the internet in 2018, compared with 81% earning under $30,000 and 98% earning $75,000 or more; usage was 65% among those without a high-school education versus 97% among college graduates. Although overall internet-use racial disparities were no longer significant, low-income people, racial minorities and less-educated people were more likely to depend on smartphones. Data-intensive tools could impose substantial costs on these users.
qs: 89% of US adults were internet users in 2018.
While there are no longer significant racial disparities in internet use, there are important differences by income and education.
People with low incomes, racial minorities and people with lower levels of education are among the groups most likely to be dependent on cell phones for personal internet access

kp.k: Language and literacy barriers reproduce existing exclusion
kp.d: The survey found that 75% of tools required English proficiency, only 25% offered other languages and only 16% supplied some material through nontext means. The report compares these features with cited estimates of 8.1% limited English proficiency and 14.5% below-basic adult literacy. Tools targeting low-income populations were as likely to rely on text as other tools, and prior research found overly advanced reading levels. The accessibility coding was permissive: some video or audio sufficed, rather than demonstrating complete accessibility.
qs: Fully 75% of existing tools require English-language facility.
Only 16% of tools provide at least some of the material offered though a means other than written text, such as a video.
If a tool provided videos or audio for some material, it was coded as usable by this standard.
Thus, people who are vision impaired, have low literacy, or are not proficient in English are poorly served by most existing tools.

kp.k: Free tools still face substantial usability barriers
kp.d: Roughly three quarters of tools were free to users; other tools required payment or charged for expanded services. Sandefur emphasizes that free provision does not itself establish accessibility because language, literacy and internet constraints can prevent use by low-income communities.
qs: Roughly three quarters of existing tools are free to users.
Many tools offer their services for free to users, while others offer some free services and then charge a fee for more extensive service, and some tools cannot be used without the user paying a fee.
Many tools that offer free service are not usable by many people in low-income communities, because of limited internet access or barriers of language or literacy.

kp.k: Provider-driven development weakens alignment with user needs
kp.d: Sandefur attributes the mismatch to uncoordinated tool development, outdated design practices and nonprofit resource constraints. Because most tools operated outside fee-for-service markets, she argues that consumer demand had less influence. Developers commonly followed provider assumptions rather than user-centered or collaborative design; nonprofits often lacked the time, expertise and money to assess needs or customize products. She recommends beginning with potential users' needs and perspectives.
qs: No organization or market currently coordinates tool development.
Development of digital tools is usually provider-driven, reflecting the interests and beliefs of those offering the service, rather than the wants and needs of the intended user populations.

Starting with the needs and perspectives of potential users of new tools would be the first step in creating a body of technologies that are more closely aligned with the justice problems Americans actually have and the kinds of assistance they want or need with those problems.

kp.k: Court coordination limits end-to-end document automation
kp.d: The report describes automatic court filing of generated forms as an emerging possibility, not a generally realized capability. Standardizing forms and securing acceptance across courts requires institutional coordination. Even formally approved documents may be rejected by courthouse personnel who retain older practices, making operational adoption rather than technical capacity a key constraint.
qs: Even when rules change formally, clerks, judges and other courthouse staff can persist in older patterns, refusing to recognize documents that are officially approved by the court system.
The barriers here are not technological, but human.

kp.k: Unauthorized-practice restrictions constrain tools' substantive assistance
kp.d: Sandefur argues that US restrictions on nonlawyer legal advice discourage diagnosis, recommended responses and other assistance beyond general information. She contrasts this with other jurisdictions, including the United Kingdom, and identifies unauthorized-practice enforcement risk as a reason tools remain limited. Citing research on nonlawyer services, she recommends evidence-guided rule revisions; the survey itself does not establish the safety or efficacy of expanded digital advice.
qs: Non-lawyers engaged in providing services that look like legal advice are at risk of the legal profession’s action against the unauthorized practice of law.
As a way of avoiding this risk, most US tools stay in the realm of “legal information,” general, publicly available information about the law and people’s rights.
This evidence base can help guide sensible revisions to the rules about unauthorized practice that would permit the expansion of what both human non-lawyers and digital tools can provide.

kp.k: Appendix records an attorney-assisted bankruptcy automation claim
kp.d: The appendix reproduces Upsolve's claim that its software guides Chapter 7 applicants and assembles official forms for light-touch attorney review before pro se filing. Upsolve claimed a reduction in attorney time from 6 hours to 1.5 hours and reported that its minimum viable product helped 35 New Yorkers discharge over $1.5 million in debt. These are attributed product claims, not independently established survey outcomes or evidence specifically of AI.
qs: Our technology guides users through the Chapter 7 bankruptcy process and assembles the official bankruptcy forms, which only need a light-touch attorney review before filing pro se.
By leveraging technology, Upsolve cuts the attorney time to file from 6 hours to 1.5 hours.
Our minimum viable product has already helped 35 New Yorkers get a fresh start, successfully discharging over $1.5 million in debt.

kp.k: Realizing digital legal empowerment requires social change
kp.d: The report's overarching conclusion is conditional: digital technologies could empower individuals and communities to identify, understand and act on justice problems, but realizing that promise at this stage depends primarily on human choices, institutional coordination, inclusive design and regulatory change rather than further technological development.
qs: Digital legal technologies hold promise to empower individuals and communities to identify, understand, and take action on their justice problems and to use the rights that are theirs under law.
At this stage in the growth of this field of activity, realizing that promise is not a technological challenge, but rather a social one.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sandefur claims that digital legal technologies can empower non-lawyers to address justice problems, but existing tools provide limited independent action and poorly match public needs. These are claims about digital legal technology generally, not findings about AI specifically.
pts.d: The report's central argument is that tools could help people identify, understand and act on justice problems, but most currently supply information, lawyer connections or isolated tasks rather than integrated assistance. Of 322 identified tools, 167 (52%) facilitate some action without attorney assistance; document production dominates this subset. Sandefur describes JustFix as a rare example that helps compile a housing complaint and sends a landlord letter. She reports no general-purpose tool combining natural-language diagnosis, options, evidence compilation and document creation or filing. The appendix includes AI-related product descriptions, but these should not be treated as independently established author findings about AI performance.

pts.k: Sandefur argues that diagnosis and response guidance could be particularly valuable because people often do not recognize their problems as legally actionable.
pts.d: The author distinguishes document generation, which usually occurs after a person recognizes a legal problem and decides to act, from earlier assistance identifying legal aspects and possible responses. She claims the concentration on documents therefore leaves most justice problems unserved by existing tools. This is an argument grounded in legal-needs research, not a measured comparison of AI diagnosis against lawyers or other services.

pts.k: Sandefur identifies design choices, resource constraints, unauthorized-practice restrictions and court coordination as the principal limits on more useful technology-enabled assistance.
pts.d: She argues that provider-driven development and nonprofit resource scarcity weaken alignment with users' needs. US restrictions on non-lawyer legal advice encourage tools to remain within general legal information rather than diagnosis or recommended action. Fragmented court practices impede standardized forms and automated filing even where formal approval exists. She proposes more user-centered development and evidence-informed revisions to unauthorized-practice rules as routes to expanded assistance. These are explanatory and conditional reform claims, not quantified causal estimates or forecasts of lawyer displacement.

pts.k: The appendix records specific AI-related service claims, but distinguishes neither their technical performance nor their effectiveness through testing.
pts.d: The appendix describes Law Mixer as immediately producing legal information from a user's description using AI and machine learning. It reproduces AI Patents' claim that natural-language input can retrieve relevant patent documents without an expert searcher; Civil Informer's prospective claim of an AI-and-expert system recommending case-specific steps; Learn Our Rights' claim to translate relevant statutes into plain English using AI; and ROSS Intelligence's claim to answer natural-language legal questions with citations. The directly quoted claims belong to the named providers, not to Sandefur as validated conclusions. Civil Informer explicitly describes a system under development.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main evidence is a descriptive inventory of 322 tools, supplemented by legal-needs, accessibility and non-lawyer-service research; it is not an AI benchmark or an evaluation of tool outcomes.
pts.d: Researchers combined existing lists, app-store searches and practitioner/funder outreach, removed duplicates from more than 600 US legal technologies, and inspected tools to identify those serving non-lawyers. They coded areas of law, functions and accessibility. Comparisons with public needs draw on Sandefur's earlier work and Legal Services Corporation surveys; accessibility comparisons use Pew, literacy, language and disability data from different years. Design and regulatory arguments cite Hagan, Rhode and Ricca, and Sandefur and Clarke, among others. Appendix AI claims are sourced to provider websites or business profiles, without reported accuracy, safety or outcome tests. Separately, the appendix quotes Upsolve's claim that automation reduces attorney filing time from six to 1.5 hours and that its minimum viable product helped 35 New Yorkers discharge over $1.5 million in debt; this is a provider-reported example of technology-assisted service, not an AI-specific finding.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern US tools as of fall 2018, published in 2019; future empowerment is conditional on social and institutional changes rather than a specified technological timetable.
pts.d: Statements about existing tools and the absence of a general-purpose integrated service are historical observations within a non-exhaustive inventory. The report supplies no date for achieving broader diagnosis, action support or automated court filing. Expansion depends on user-centered design, development resources, accessible interfaces, court acceptance and changes to restrictions on non-lawyer assistance. The author acknowledges some technological limitations but locates the primary constraints in human institutions. Appendix claims use differing present and prospective language and should not be read as evidence that all listed capabilities were operational.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are members of the public with unmet legal needs and non-lawyer helpers; barriers particularly affect already underserved communities.
pts.d: The report focuses on individuals acting on their own problems and social workers, community organizers, court staff and social-service providers helping others. Potential benefits include independent document preparation, evidence collection, diagnosis and dispute resolution. Low-income people, those with less education, people with limited English or literacy, and visually impaired users may be excluded by connectivity and interface requirements. Racial disparities are discussed in the mode of internet access, especially smartphone dependence, not as significant disparities in overall internet use in 2018. The survey reports that 75% of tools require English-language facility, only 16% provide at least some non-text material, and roughly three quarters are free. Free access therefore does not ensure usability. Legal aid organizations face development-resource constraints, while courts and the profession influence the permissible and practical scope of services.
